messages.subject_clean: predict() help to estimate abundance using a robust n-mixture design
messages.body_plain:
Megan,

I don't think I have an answer for you, but I'll attempt to clarify the question so that one of the more knowledgeable unmarked gurus can swoop in and correct me.  (I echo your thanks to those to contribute, and whose knowledge is well beyond mine!).

It seems like you're trying to answer a question across multiple dimensions at once, i.e., at different sites during different seasons and with varying detection covariable values (temperature), all in one data frame.  My understanding is that because the new data frame for predict is only a table in two dimensions, you can't vary more than one thing at a time.  So, I believe you can set up a data frame to examine differences in your 19 sites at a set temperature during a set season.  Or, you can look at the average across your sites at a set temperature during various seasons.  Or, you could look at the effect of temperature during a given season at an 'average' or one particular site.  I don't think you can do all at once, but by predicting and then graphing these predictions, varying one variable at a time, you can get a sense of the relationships.  And note that you could choose an average, or a meaningful value (we will only survey at temperatures above X value, so set temp as X in the predict dataframe and then estimate N across all sites), or any of the seasons.  It seems like unmarked is predicting across 3 variables at once, which might be mathematically correct but is very hard to interpret meaningfully.

Is that the crux of the issue, or do I misunderstand the question?

-Alex

messages.subject: Pcountopen dynamics
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

Just wanted to first say that this group has been very helpful in answering a lot of the questions I’ve had while analysing my n mixture model data, so thank you!

I do have a couple of questions regarding the open population N-mixture model that I haven’t been able to find answers to, even after reading the vignettes and Dail & Madsen’s and Royle’s paper. I’m sorry if they’re daft questions, I’m fairly new to this:

1. Dynamics type eg. trend, ricker, gompertz: How do you decide on the right dynamics type? Is it by AIC? If so, some dynamics types make more sense biologically, such as ricker and Gompertz. My best performing model is a trend dynamics type, so what does that say about the population I’m studying? Is there a paper I can read more about this?

2. Initially, my best performing model was a Gompertz dynamics type, and the gamma was 0.508 and omega is 37.9. According to the vignette, this means my population growth rate is 0.508 and carrying capacity is 37.9. For carrying capacity, is it an average and do I multiply the value with the number of sites?

Would really appreciate any help in this, either by answering directly or pointing me in the right direction in terms of resources. Thanks again!

messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Pcountopen dynamics
messages.body_plain:
Dear Inuyasha (?),

I make a stab at your first question, anybody please correct me if you disagree or if I am wrong.

I find that in many situations, the most important criterion for model selection should be a combination of your biological insight and the goals of your modelling. So, if you think that density-dependent (DD) regulation is a strong feature of your population (of what ?), then I’d choose either ricker or gompertz and then do data-based selection between them using the AIC. Similarly, if you’re interested in DD and would like to estimate things like carrying capacity, then evidently you’d need a model that incorporates this feature.

On the other hand, if you’re just after some descriptive accommodation of population change and are not sure how close or far your population may be from a limit, then perhaps the simple trend model (which I think is simple exponential growth without DD) may be OK, and if it is preferred by AIC, then this may be the one to go with.

Not sure about your second question.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: Today's SDM quiz
messages.body_plain:
Probably too simple an explanation, by my gut reaction is because there are more data being used to estimate the slopes in the abundance model, so detection bias doesn’t become an all or nothing scenario as it is in p/a. So, the slopes can still be estimated in an abundance model even under p<1.

--

messages.subject: Re: Today's SDM quiz
messages.body_plain:
I would say it's because the contamination is one-sided with presence/absence data, which causes the effect size to be underestimated on average.  With abundance, the imperfect detection is an equal opportunity phenomenon so the relative comparisons still hold.  The stark difference in accuracy/precision also highlights how hungry the logistic regression is for data, and the greater relative value of counts over 0/1s.

I bet that even if you model p, the occupancy slopes will be slightly underestimated.

messages.body_plain:
occmatx should be numeric (0, 1, NA), but based on the output you show, it looks like it is a matrix of character strings ("0", "1", "NA"). If that's the case you should convert all the elements to numeric with code like

occmatx_new <- matrix(as.numeric(occmatx), ncol=ncol(occmatx))

double checking of course that everything was converted correctly.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Changing scale on plot
messages.body_plain:
Hello there Sara,

yes I was able to build the plot. I ended up not using these plots but the code that worked for me was this:

# Predict colonization for the final model
final_pred_col <- predict(final_mod, type = 'col')
head(final_pred_col)

# Create covariate to have original scale values
npred <- 400  # 400 is the number of sites I have
x.lst.org <http://x.lst.org> <- as.data.frame(seq(22, 51, length.out = npred))
colnames(x.cov1.org <http://x.cov1.org>) <- c("cov1")
head(x.cov1.org <http://x.cov1.org>)

# Get data frame with range of scaled cov1 values
nd2_col <- data.frame(("cov1" = (seq(min(unmarkedMultFrame_ev@yearlySiteCovs$cov1), max(unmarkedMultFrame_ev@yearlySiteCovs$cov1), length.out=400))))
colnames(nd2_col) <- c("cov1")
head(nd2_col)

# Predict final model against scaled values
final_pred_col <- predict(final_mod, type = 'col', newdata= nd2_col)
print(predictions<-cbind( final_pred_col , x.cov1.org <http://x.cov1.org>))
head(predictions)

# Plot predicted values against ORIGINAL cov1 values (not scaled)
plot(1, xlim=range(predictions$cov1), ylim=c(0,1), type="n", axes=T, xlab="Covariate 1",

     pch=20, ylab="Colonization Probability",

     cex.lab=1.25, cex.main=1.75)

lines(predictions$cov1, predictions$Predicted, col="blue", lwd=2)
lines(predictions$cov1, predictions$lower, lty=2, col="black")
lines(predictions$cov1, predictions$upper, lty=2, col="black")

The final result should be something like this:

Best,
Pinto
